aboutAuthor: David Ogilvy, 'the Father of Advertising,' founded Ogilvy & Mather and created some of the most famous campaigns of the 20th century. Confessions of an Advertising Man is his candid manual on running the business and writing copy that sells.

points.heading: The consumer is not a moron
points.body: Ogilvy's most quoted commandment: treat your audience as your wife. Research-informed respect beats cleverness — advertising that wins awards but doesn't sell is 'the folly of the pursuit of applause.'

points.heading: Big ideas come from big research
points.body: Ogilvy was a researcher first (at Gallup) and demanded facts before inspiration: study the product, the competitors, and what customers already believe. Positioning — what the product does and for whom — must be decided before a single line of copy.

points.heading: Brand image is a long-term asset
points.body: Every advertisement is an investment in the long-term symbol of the brand. Short-sighted promotions erode image; consistent quality builds equity that compounds like capital. 'Unless your campaign contains a big idea, it will pass like a ship in the night.'

points.heading: Write headlines that do the heavy lifting
points.body: Five times as many people read headlines as body copy. The headline should promise a benefit, contain the brand name, and be specific: numbers, facts, and news beat vague poetry every time.

points.heading: Long copy sells more than short copy
points.body: Ogilvy's data showed readership falls off slowly — people will read long ads if they're interested. Fill every ad with useful information; the reader's time is spent only when the selling is done.

points.heading: Build an agency of gentlemen with brains
points.body: Ogilvy managed through candor, high standards, and zero politics. His rules for leadership: hire people better than yourself, praise in public and criticize in private, and fire office politicians without mercy.

insights: Ogilvy wrote the book at his Château de Touffou as a retirement summary — it sold over a million copies.
His Rolls-Royce headline ('At 60 miles an hour the loudest noise comes from the electric clock') remains a copywriting benchmark.
He famously refused clients whose products he wouldn't use himself.
conclusion: Confessions distills advertising into respect for the consumer, discipline from research, and patience with brand-building. Sell or be fired — Ogilvy's creed — still separates professionals from entertainers.
